Is the Mk7 Volkswagen Golf the best 
Golf there will ever be? I think there
is a good argument for it, and I'm going to try

in 2013, so it's been around a long time
and it has been superseded by the Mk8. I've 
always admired the Golf Mk7 from afar but
until now I've never driven one and I've always 
seen it as the spiritual successor to the Mk4
- which I've done a review on already. The Mk7 
is a car that a lot of people have been saying
it's like the last 'proper Golf' - the last 
Golf that fits all the criteria of what a Golf
should be - which is a very refined and quality 
and luxury car for a reasonable price.
When I get in this car and drive it, what are my 
initial Impressions? The first thing is that
it's just really refined in here. Now that's 
a word that car journalists throw around
and it does encompass a lot of different 
things. Essentially, it's quiet, it's smooth, it
glides over bumps in the road. When you're going at speed there's not much wind or road noise.
A lack of noise, vibration and harshness -that's the 
official term that they use. You really can tell
that Volkswagen have made that their priority 
with this car. It's not the softest spongiest
smoothest ride ever, but it's got a very 
relaxing demeanour to it. You can't
really hear the engine, even if I drive it 
like an old person with the revs too high.
Inside the cabin of the Mk7, it's as always 
a very sensible affair from Volkswagen - no
Italian flair or French quirkiness, it's all 
just very business-like, sensible, well laid out dashboard.
By no means does it look bad. One 
disappointing thing with this being an older
design is that the infotainment screen is down 
quite low, and I much prefer having that up here
so that you don't have to take your eye too far 
off the road. I quite like in this particular model
the brushed metal effect that we've got going 
on here. The dashboard is slightly angled
towards the driver as well, which is a vaguely sporty 
touch, along with this flat bottomed steering
wheel which is obviously... pointless. These cloth 
seats are fairly comfortable - good side lateral
support. One thing I would say is that there's no 
lumbar adjustment and I think that probably some
of the Golfs - the higher spec ones - you could get it. 
I can feel my back arching slightly the
wrong way into this seat. So this car is mid-spec, 
it's a 'Match' - means that it's got things like auto lights
and it's actually got heated seats 
which is nice. You've got an auto-dim rear view
mirror, dual zone climate control, this one's got 
radar cruise control as well. Every single Golf
Mk7, right from the beginning will come 
with air conditioning and 4x electric
windows. Most other things are on the higher
trim levels but of course most Golfs were sold at
a higher trim level, so unless you're finding a Golf S, which is the base you'll have other things.
Now of course with this being a modern car, it's got 
an electronic handbrake. Quite a quiet one actually
and obviously it comes off when you drive off.
It's also got Auto Hold which is a Volkswagen
thing. It's nice when you need to do a hill start 
because you don't have to worry about that, it'll
just hold you on the brakes until you set off but 
also it'll hold you when you're facing downhill as well.
The infotainment system in the middle here, it's 
got a decent processor in it I can tell because it
responds dead quick to everything and you can 
zoom in and out on the sat nav and it doesn't
lag. You've got some little buttons either side 
of the screen which you got on all of the Golfs
except for the biggest screen. You can set all 
manner of things in the options for the car,
it's quite customizable. Now I've said this many 
times in many videos, this one at least has Android Auto,
now I presume that's something that they 
introduced in the later 'Mk7.5' and on.
Android Auto, Apple Carplay are really important I think 
in a modern car because the software is
always much better when it's built by Google or 
Apple. In front of me I've got controls on the
steering wheel for the infotainment and radio, and I've also got all the cruise control on
the steering wheel. Volkswagen did have it 
on a stalk and I much prefer having it on here.
The styling of this car, I actually 
really like it - I think it's a perfect design
for the Volkswagen Golf. It's how a modern Golf 
should look. It's got all the right sort
of features - it's got the very square sharp lines,
and the the right kink at the back in the C-pillar.
Quite an understated design, but it's quite 
a good looking car in my opinion. It's a very

other optional extras, but they didn't change 
the basic way that the car drives. I'm pleased
to report that there is a three-door version,  it was mostly the Golf GTI and Golf R that
had the three-door body shell. I always like to 
see a three-door and that's something that has
disappeared now. But you also have an estate

it's got more power than the 1.2 turbo which

115 horsepower and 0-60mph in 9.3 seconds, so it's 
perfectly adequate performance from that tiny one
litre engine. All petrol and diesel Golfs were

action on it as well. Glovebox is air conditioned,

Oh these things? yeah these

got for you mate, because you keep banging on
about how good the Mk4 is I thought you'd 
probably need a pair of these. There you go...
Fair enough, ooh yeah it's like it's 1997

So head and leg room - I've got plenty of 
headroom, the leg room is just enough for me to sit

actually, but don't tell him that. Little pockets
back here as well, with the 
carpet-y stuff which is nice.
There are two vents on the back of the 
centre console, the seats fold 60/40 and
there is an armrest here and a ski hatch 
so you can get in the boot and put your
skis through there. Two little lights 
up here and back to you!
Cheers mate.
So let's say you do want to take this car out on a 
twisty road and have a bit of fun with it, how
does it handle? It's all right! It's much better 
than the Golf MkIV that I reviewed, as I said
in that review, it was Boaty McBoatface.
This is very much not Boaty McBoatface.
The steering feels fairly accurate, definitely set up to be a comfortable car, and it's not
really focused on handling but it's good enough 
that you could you can have fun with it.
Now, used Golfs can be quite expensive to buy and they've 
got quite good residuals so at least it
means that they'll hold value when you come to 
sell yours, but they are also pretty affordable
to run because the tax on pretty much every Golf 
in the UK apart from the performance ones is £20
or £30 a year to tax - now that only goes up 
to 2017, so any car newer than that it'll just be
that flat rate. They're not bad to insure, this 
one's pretty low - group 17 or
something like that. A lot of people say about 
the Golf - and I do agree - that it's 'classless'.
You could quite easily see it in the hand of almost 
any type of driver - could be a rich person's car,
someone who just wants to fly under the radar 
but still wants a nice car to actually drive
around in, but it could also be a family 
car, a boy racer car, grandma's car. If you've been
watching a few of my videos and I keep 
popping up on the home feed, please do think about

But to me it makes a big difference.
In conclusion then - is this the best Golf that 
there will ever be? Now obviously I can't tell you what

from a Golf - it's comfortable, it's refined,
it's understatedly good looking. The Mk8 doesn't

the moment I think I'll give them equal standing.

The 7th generation Volkswagen Golf introduced
a new chassis and lineup across its range,
at the top of the specification was the R
model that had first arrived in the previous
MK6 generation.
VW made a special effort to really stand out
their top spec model in the 7th generation
and so with the boardroom signed off and the
engineering team aiming to make the Golf R
the performance car for every situation the
new R arrived in 2013 and was initially offered
in both three and five-door configuration
in some markets.
A facelift was shown to the world in November
2016, many known this as the MK7.5 model and
most dealerships had the model ready for deliveries
to customers at the beginning of 2017.
Differences include a new style to the front
and rear lighting, and bumper details, infotainment
upgrades along with a digital dashboard that
was optional in some markets and standard
in others, and a performance upgrade that
we’ll cover later in the guide.
In North America, this was a 2018 model year.
After the facelift the three-door option began
to be dropped from most markets and by 2019
it had almost disappeared.
However, the manual gearbox remained an option,
even as more and more buyers agreed with automotive
journalists of the day and opted for the DSG
transmission.
One option that has become especially desirable
on the used market is the Spekrum program
Golf R model.
These were offered in a range of 40 colours.
Less than 500 were produced with just shy
of 200 going to North America, however, some
popular YouTubers and automotive outlets signed
up for a model that brought added attention
to the R model, before it was then discontinued
for the arrival of the MK8.
Today the MK7 and 7.5 Golf R has become popular
with tuners and those wanting to squeeze some
extra potential from their hot hatchback.
Volkswagen themselves nearly answered the
demand with the R400 model.
This was planned for release with 395bhp but
as is sometimes the way with automotive projects
that customers want, but manufacturers cannot
supply, the R400 was mothballed by VW as the
emissions scandal swept across news outlets
leading to a rethink of pumping out an attention-grabbing
high-performance Golf.
Golf R models are distinct from the rest of
the Golf range not just because of the power
and styling upgrades, but the Haldex 4motion
all-wheel drive is offered as standard.
Although the R is not the only Golf to be
offered with an all-wheel drive system, it
is the only one to utilize the system for
increased performance.
The ability for the rear wheels to decouple
when cruising or not demanded by the terrain
means increased fuel economy.
The R also sits 20mm lower to the ground on
a stiffer suspension set-up, from experience
Volkswagen managed to tune in just enough
increased feel and sharpened handling without
entirely sacrificing the primary ride of the
vehicle, although the secondary ride is somewhat
harsher than the rest of the range.
Interestingly, the Golf GTI of this generation
pulls off this compromise even better, likely
due to lighter weight and the rear suspension
tuning on a chassis that was developed primarily

The seventh-generation golf GTI was built
on the MQB platform that is ubiquitous across
the Volkswagen Group and was revealed in Berlin,
Germany on September the 4th of 2012.
The GTI began deliveries in 2013 and all models
are Euro 6 emissions compliant.
Throughout
Its production the Golf GTI was only offered
with a third generation 2-litre four-cylinder
engine, coded EA888.
A three and five door variant were available
at launch for some markets, and continued
late into the life of the Golf GTI however
for some markets the three door was dropped
after a facelift in 2017, while others had
a limited supply or special editions that
remained in three-door.
By the end of production, the three-door was
gone and in the eight generation all Golf
models are now five-door only.
The facelift model, commonly referred to as
the MK7.5 GTI was seen as a new Golf by VW,
but most informally referred to it as a facelifted
MK7.5 and it has won a large enthusiast following
with many believing the 7.5 gen is the peak
of the Volkswagen Golf GTI as the eighth generation
moved to a new styling and interior design
although it stuck with the same platform.
There are many changes to the MK7.5 but they
are easily identified by a digital dash and
larger infotainment screen and revised exterior
styling.
The GTI was sold with a variety of power outputs
depending on options or special edition models.
The base GTI made 217bhp, with the most powerful
creating 306bhp, but we’ll come onto these
further on in the video.
During the production of the Volkswagen Golf
a variety of version aside from the standard
model were offered including an optional Performance
Pack which is highly desirable on the used
market.
There was also special edition models including
the 2016 GTI Club sport that was sold with
optional Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires
and a limited slip differential.
This was followed by the GTI Clubsport S in
the same year, which was a three door only
edition with more power and uprated suspension
and subframe compared to the regular Clubsport
model, a total of 400 were produced.
There was also a TCR model released in 2019.
Some markets were also offered a ‘rabbit
edition’ in 2019 that featured styling tweaks
and a rabbit logo.
First up in our guide are the areas you should
look out for across the life of the seventh
generation Golf GTI, as ever our lists are
non-exhaustive and so if you know of any common
issue that we have missed please add them
to the comments below.
First up there is a note for owners and potential
buyers of manual transmission models that
the clutch is generally considered at its
power limit from the factory, if you have
any intent on tuning it will likely reduce
the service life of the clutch and an uprated
model should be considered to handle the additional
power.
Vehciles equipped with a sunroof may have
had the seal either wrongly fitted or an inadequately
sized part may have been fitted from factory.
Several service bulletins and recall notices
should have resolved effected models, however
it is worth check around the seal on a used
example.
Electrical damage has occurred on some vehicles
where the issue has not been resolved
Washer fluid sensors are susceptible to failure
if the wrong fluid is used due to their design.
If you get see and engine management light
that points to washer fluid this is the most
likely cause.
Parcel shelf clips are susceptible to breaking
if put under too much stress while load carrying.
They can also become damaged without completely
breaking which will cause a rattle.
Water ingress into the passenger footwell
has been reported caused by a crack in the
mounting bracket for the door speaker.
Look carefully for any signs of discolored
carpet or damp patches on the passenger side
when viewing a vehicle.
If you experience poor heater performance
or the fan speed is weak on all setting then
the blower motor has likely failed.
Code B10BE will show up on diagnostic equipment
if this is the case.
If this issue only arises when using the air
conditioning and is accompanied by a noise
in the engine bay then the problem is with
the air conditioning solenoid valve.
Any clunking sound from the front end that
is not caused by worn dampers or bushings
is likely from the subframe bolts.
When looking to buy a vehicle make sure the
latch and release cable for the bonnet release
is operable without a large amount of effort.
If so the mechanisms is under additional stress
and likely to fail.
A broken bonnet release cable is a common
issue across the 7th generation Golf, but
as we highlight in all our guides, for an
issue to be classed as common it is usually
between 1-5% of production vehicles.
Finally the oil pan is plastic, this in itself
shouldn’t be much of a problem although
heat cycling the pan has caused a small number
of owners to report the need for replacement.
It was difficult to identify whether these
were just meticulous owners that had noticed
a fractional difference or oil pans on the
edge of failure, however the drain plug is
also plastic and must be replaced after every
oil change rather than reused.
Expect oil leaks if the plastic plug is reused.
Next up are the common faults with the engine,
and as a single unit is used we will start
by mentioning issues likely to impact all
power output models, and then specify and
particular issues.
First up though a reminder that if you want
more from the Miles Driven we have a website
and a podcast, and if you are enjoying the
video then a like really does make a huge
difference the discoverability of videos on
youtube.
As ever we appreciate every subscriber to
our channel
The 2.0-litre third generation EA888 engine
found in the Golf GTI is a cast iron block
with aluminum head with a bore of 82.5mm and
a stroke of 92.8mm for a total displacement
of 1984cc.
Fuel consumption varies slightly depending
on specification and age but official figures
hover between 43.7mpg and 47.1mpg.
One of the reasons for this relatively low
fuel consumption is that the third generation
EA888 motor adds water-cooling to the exhaust
manifold speed up the time it takes to warm
up from a cold start and then to maintain
temperatures while operating.
The early Golf GTI produces 217bhp, with the
performance pack boosting this to 227bhp.
The performance pack also adds a limited slip
differential named VAQ along with uprated
brakes.
The Clubsport model produced 306bhp becoming
the most powerful Golf GTI, a record that
the late TCR model was unable to beat due
to the additional exhaust restrictions introduced
in 2018, the TCR produced 286bhp.
First up you should note that PCV failure
is one of the more common issues found on
the EA888 engine and a common side effect
with be the failure of the rear main seal,
causing an oil leak.
Deterioration of the plastic housing for the
thermostat is one of the most common areas
for coolant loss.
If you can smell coolant but struggle to visually
see a leak then this is likely culprit.
The other likely cause is a failing or failed
water pump.
Turbo charger failure is a known fault of
models fitted with the 06K 145 702N unit fitted
in many 2015to 2017 models.
A revision to the design was made after this
date and so if the unit fitted to your car
ends 722 then the vehicle was either fitted
from factory with the updated unit or has
been replaced at some point in the vehicles
history.
The seal from turbo to manifold seems to be
the weak spot and the reason for the 702N
turbo failures.
Fault codes P0300, P0301, P0302, P0303, P0304
are all likely signs of an ignition coil pack
failure.
A side note is that the end number relates
to each cylinder, so for example the P0303
would be an issue detected in cylinder number
three.
The code ending zero is a multiple cylinder
misfire.
Other signs of this failure are poor engine
running and rough idle.
Carbon build up on valves is a side effect
of the injection system on these engines.
Owners generally believe every 60,000 miles
the valves need to manually cleaned.
Some believe walnut blasting is better than
sand blasting , there are other types of media
that can also be used.
If you believe one way or another is better
let us known in the comments.
Some owners running premium fuel report better
longevity and less carbon build up but this
point becomes contentious with others believing
use of additives on a regular basis better,
let us know your thoughts in the comments.
Finally, some cars produced for model year
2015 and 2016 had a recall code 20Y6 to replace
a pump in the fuel tank for the EVAP system.
Clogged charcoal cannisters are a sign of
failure and the total number of vehicles recalled
for this issue exceeded 100,000.
If we’ve missed any other common faults
please let us know to help in the comments
to help owners and potential buyers.
For our picks we would suggest those with
a lower budget purchase a good condition early
standard model and then improve the vehicle
rather than limiting themselves to one with
the upgraded performance pack as these demand
a premium and so better condition standard
models will likely be a better buy unless
you find a great deal.
If shopping with a higher budget go for the
mk7.5 wherever possible.
If a three door works for your needs that
is what we would go for however a five door
does add practicality.
